doc.title: Vince DiMartino interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 8, 2025

title: Recitals, brass quintet, and playing behind Aretha Franklin
summary: He talks of trumpet and organ recitals, concentration in brass quintet, and listening during rests behind Aretha Franklin.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: Exactly. And of course I love playing brass quintets, I love playing recitals. I’ve played, I’ve probably — 150 to 200 recit — maybe more. I never counted. I played trumpet and organ for 25 years with a good friend of mine at U.K. We had a National Endowment for the Arts grant and we played all over the country just doing recitals. And I played at least 10 to 15 recitals a year, I must have done at least 400 then. Yeah. So I probably, but it was never like I was counting them it was just something I looked forward to.

Did you ever have the experience, especially when you started out, playing, you know, contract things to play behind a performer. This happened to me when Aretha Franklin came here. © Fillius Jazz Archive -16-
Yeah. And I got to play in the horn section. And I found that I can’t look at her because if I do I’m going to get enthralled and I’m going to miss like eight measures.

Yeah. There’s a certain — well you develop a work ethic so to speak — maybe it’s probably a work ethic, or there’s probably a better word for it than that, but it would be like when you do certain things. When I play brass quintet there’s nothing I’m thinking about except where I’m going. And that’s why the concentration factor in brass quintet playing is very challenging. It’s harder than playing recitals with just a piano and trumpet. Maybe not — physically it’s just as much, almost the same, okay? Because you never rest much. If you’re playing first trumpet you just play all the time. And you’re playing the high part you know so that that concentration — so when you play a show like Aretha Franklin there’s a lot of places you don’t play. So that’s when I listen to Aretha Franklin. The rest of the time — and there’s really, there’s another part to it, the part that makes your trumpet work, see? Let’s see I’ve got that background thing there. [whistles] See? The trumpet is not a visual instrument. Music is not visual, it’s sonic. So if you have to look at the music and see Cs and Gs that takes too long. That’s too long.
